title: Edible seaweed: types and nutritional value

seo.title: Edible seaweed: types and nutritional value
seo.meta_description: Nori, wakame, kombu, dulse, and sea lettuce have very different nutrition. Learn how red, brown, and green seaweeds differ in protein, fiber, salt, and iodine.
seo.search_intent: Learn the main types of edible seaweed and how their nutrition differs

excerpt: Edible seaweeds include red, brown, and green species with very different profiles. Dried seaweeds are generally low in fat and rich in fiber and minerals; red nori can be relatively high in protein, while brown wakame and especially kombu tend to contain more iodine. The species name matters far more than the word “seaweed.”
content_html:
“Seaweed is nutritious” is about as specific as “vegetables are nutritious.” The category includes foods that can differ dramatically. Nori, wakame, kombu, dulse, and sea lettuce should not be treated as nutritionally interchangeable.

Three broad groups show up on the plate

Red seaweeds include nori/Pyropia-Porphyra and dulse. Brown seaweeds include wakame, kombu, arame, and many kelps. Green seaweeds include sea lettuce in the genus Ulva.

Those groups have different pigments, cell-wall polysaccharides, and mineral-accumulation patterns.

Nori can be surprisingly protein-rich

In one dry-matter analysis of edible seaweeds, nori contained about 32% protein, compared with about 19% in dulse and 10% in the wakame sample.

A sheet is only a few grams, so that does not translate into 32 g protein at the table. Three grams of a 32%-protein nori would provide about 1 g.

Brown seaweeds can be especially fiber-rich

The same study measured about 41% total dietary fiber in dried wakame and about 31% in nori. Brown-seaweed alginates and other structural carbohydrates contribute to that profile.

Because dried seaweed reabsorbs a lot of water, nutrition per 100 g drops sharply after soaking even though the food has not lost all those nutrients.

Iodine is the nutrient that needs the most caution

A commercial survey found 29–46 mcg/g in nori, 94–185 mcg/g in wakame, and 241–4,921 mcg/g in kombu.

The U.S. adult upper limit is 1,100 mcg/day. A small amount of high-iodine kombu can exceed it, so recommending a generic tablespoon of “seaweed” makes little sense without knowing the species.

Salt and other minerals vary too

Seaweed can contain sodium, calcium, magnesium, iron, and trace elements accumulated from seawater. Species, growing location, season, age, and processing all change the values.

Fat is usually low—often around 1–2% dry matter in macroalgae studies—even though the small lipid fraction can include interesting fatty acids.

Preparation changes the numbers

Drying concentrates nutrients per gram. Rehydration dilutes them with water. Washing, soaking, and boiling can leach soluble minerals, including some iodine.

How to use the category sensibly

Nori works as sheets or flakes; wakame is usually rehydrated for soup or salad; kombu brings umami to broths but deserves particular iodine awareness; dulse and sea lettuce work well as seasonings.

Learn the species name and the dry amount you are using. With seaweed, those details tell you far more than a generic mineral claim.

faq.question: Which seaweed is highest in protein?
faq.answer: Red seaweeds such as nori often stand out. One dry-matter study measured about 32% protein in nori, though normal servings are only a few grams.

faq.question: Which seaweed is highest in iodine?
faq.answer: Brown kelps such as kombu are generally far higher than nori and usually higher than wakame, with enormous product-to-product variation.

faq.question: Is seaweed high in fat?
faq.answer: Generally no. Macroalgae are usually low-fat foods; fiber and minerals are more prominent features.

faq.question: Does soaking reduce iodine?
faq.answer: It can. Iodine is water-soluble, so soaking or boiling may leach some out, depending on species and method.
